content: Alcohol consumption among young individuals is associated with a variety of shortand long-term health risks, making it a significant concern for healthcare providers, policymakers, educators, youth workers, and parents. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of family-based prevention programs in reducing alcohol use or problematic drinking behaviors in school-aged children and adolescents up to 18 years of age. Specifically, the review assessed three types of interventions: universal programs targeting all children regardless of risk, selective programs for children at higher risk of alcohol use or problematic drinking, and indicated programs for children who have already initiated alcohol use or are consuming alcohol regularly. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, ERIC, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar, covering literature up to June 2018. Additional searches included clinical trial registries and references from related systematic reviews. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster RCTs (C-RCTs) involving parents of school-aged children. These interventions were psychosocial or educational in nature and involved parents either alone or in combination with their children. Comparisons were made against no intervention or alternative interventions, such as child-only programs, to isolate the effects of parent-focused components. The review included 46 studies with a total of 39,822 participants. Of these, 27 studies were classified as universal interventions, 12 as selective interventions, and seven as indicated interventions. Meta-analyses were conducted to evaluate outcomes such as the prevalence, frequency, and volume of alcohol use. However, the overall quality of evidence was rated as low or very low, and there was significant, unexplained heterogeneity across studies. When comparing any family-based intervention to no intervention or standard care, no significant effect was observed on the prevalence of alcohol use (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.08 to 0.08; 12 studies; 7,490 participants; I² = 57%; low-quality evidence). Similarly, no effect was found on the frequency of alcohol use (SMD -0.31, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.21; 8 studies; 1,835 participants; I² = 96%; very low-quality evidence). The impact on the volume of alcohol consumption was minimal (SMD -0.14, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.00; 5 studies; 1,825 participants; I² = 42%; low-quality evidence). When comparing combined parent/family and adolescent interventions to adolescent-only interventions, no significant differences were found in alcohol use prevalence (SMD -0.39, 95% CI -0.91 to 0.14; 4 studies; 5,640 participants; I² = 99%; very low-quality evidence) or frequency (SMD -0.16, 95% CI -0.42 to 0.09; 4 studies; 915 participants; I² = 73%; very low-quality evidence). No pooled data were available for the volume of alcohol use in this comparison. Subgroup analyses of universal, selective, and indicated interventions yielded consistent results, and no adverse effects were reported in any of the included studies. In conclusion, the findings of this review do not provide clear evidence of the effectiveness of family-based prevention programs in reducing alcohol use among young people. While there were slight variations in outcomes, the overall heterogeneity and limitations in the quality of evidence preclude definitive conclusions. Further independent, high-quality studies are needed to strengthen the evidence base and clarify the marginal effects observed in this review.
